before.text: Altitude commonly influences temperature in the troposphere: higher sites are generally cooler than comparable lower sites. The main reason is that the lower atmosphere is heated mainly from below: sunlight warms the ground, and the ground then heats the air above it, so air farther above the land surface is cooler. Air at height is also thinner (less dense) and holds less heat. On average, temperature falls by about 6.5°C for each 1,000 m of height. A temperature inversion can reverse the usual decrease over a layer, so the relation is a broad tendency rather than an absolute rule for every height interval. A mountain summit and a sheltered valley floor may also have different local exposure and night-time conditions.

after.text: Altitude commonly influences temperature in the troposphere: higher sites are generally cooler than comparable lower sites. The lower atmosphere receives much of its heat from the warmed ground. Air rising into lower pressure expands and cools, helping produce the usual fall of temperature with height. The average environmental decrease is about 6.5°C per 1,000 m; this describes an average temperature profile, not the cooling rate of every rising parcel. An inversion can reverse the decrease within a layer. A mountain summit and a sheltered valley floor can also differ in exposure and night-time cooling.

before.prompt: How far do you agree that providing free antiretroviral treatment is the most important effort the Namibian government makes against HIV and AIDS?
before.canonical_answer: Agree to a large extent. Free ART in public facilities since 2003 keeps people living with HIV alive and able to work, cuts AIDS deaths among 15 to 49 year olds and means fewer children are orphaned. People on effective treatment do not pass HIV on sexually, so treatment also prevents new infections. However, ART alone does not stop people becoming infected: free condoms, testing, prevention of mother-to-child transmission and awareness campaigns are needed to reduce new cases, and treatment is a large lifelong cost. Overall ART is the most important single effort for saving lives, but it works best combined with prevention.

before.canonical_answer: Agree to a large extent. Zambezi borders Zambia and Botswana and lies very close to Zimbabwe, and the Trans-Caprivi Highway carries trucks through Katima Mulilo into Zambia. Truck drivers, migrant workers and traders spend long periods away from home and may have several partners, spreading HIV along the route and in border towns. Ohangwena, also high, borders Angola and is densely settled, while thinly populated Kunene is low, which supports the movement explanation. However, other factors matter: women's lower social and economic status raises their risk, and prevalence also reflects how long people survive on treatment. Zambezi's estimate also has a wide uncertainty range (17.5 to 27.0%). Mobility is the main explanation, but not the only one.

before.prompt: How far do you agree that communal conservancies have made wildlife use in Namibia sustainable?
before.canonical_answer: Agree to a large extent. Since 1996 communities that register a conservancy gain rights over wildlife and tourism, so animals have value to them and they have a reason to protect rather than kill them. Annual game counts set hunting and use quotas, community game guards monitor wildlife and report poaching, and tourism and hunting income pays for this work. Elephant numbers rose from about 7,600 in 1995 to about 23,600 in 2016. However, counts in surveyed areas have fallen since 2012 through drought, animal movement and suspected poaching, and households that lose crops or livestock may gain little. Decision: conservancies have greatly improved sustainability, but it depends on rainfall, enforcement and fairer sharing of costs and benefits.

before.text: A star dune has several arms or ridges radiating from a central high area, producing a multi-armed plan form. Star dunes form where winds blow from several directions during the year. Each wind pushes sand back towards the centre, so the dune grows upward instead of moving across the desert, and each arm develops its own slip face. In the Namib Sand Sea, star dunes occur on the eastern side around Sossusvlei, where some are more than 300 m high. It is not identified merely by being high, red or located in a desert. A plan showing three or more arms meeting around a central peak provides more discriminating evidence than colour. The number and length of arms can vary, and their exact angles need not form a perfect geometric star.

before.text: Seif (linear) dunes are found in the dune belt near Swakopmund, and linear dunes dominate inland across much of the Namib Sand Sea. They form where strong winds blow from the south for much of the year and winds from a second direction blow at other times. Each wind piles sand onto one flank, so the ridge does not move forward as a crescent but grows in length along the average (resultant) direction of the two winds, producing long, parallel ridges. The sand comes mainly from the Orange River: it is carried into the Atlantic Ocean, moved north along the coast by waves and currents, and blown inland by southerly winds. Sparse vegetation and dry, loose sand let the wind move it freely.

before.prompt: Explain how a fall in the volume of water can make an ephemeral river deposit its load as it flows across a sandy, permeable bed.
before.canonical_answer: Water seeps into the sandy, permeable bed and evaporates, so the volume of flowing water falls downstream. With less water the river has less energy. before.text: Velocity is speed of flow, commonly expressed in metres per second. Discharge is volume passing a cross-section per unit time, commonly cubic metres per second. The two are related through cross-sectional area but are not identical. A channel can become wider and deeper as discharge increases, so a change in volume does not determine velocity without considering channel geometry. Likewise, a narrow constriction may have rapid flow even where the river’s overall gradient is gentle. Volume still matters for deposition. When the volume of water falls, the river has less energy and can no longer carry all its load, so it deposits some of it. Volume falls in the dry season and after a flood, when water evaporates in hot, dry areas, when it seeps into a sandy or permeable bed, and when people abstract it. Many Namibian rivers are ephemeral and lose water as they flow. During the floods studied on the Kuiseb River in the Namib, the water shrank downstream and all the transported material was deposited in the lower river; no water or sediment reached the Atlantic Ocean.

before.prompt: Describe the swash/backwash sequence that produces longshore drift.
before.canonical_answer: Waves driven by the prevailing wind approach the beach at an angle, so the swash carries material diagonally up the beach. The backwash returns it straight down the slope under gravity. Repeated swash and backwash move the material in a zigzag along the coast.

(f) H1 is supported by 1:10 versus 1:20; these are sampled profiles, not every place/date. before.heading: Pebble selection, size and shape
before.text: A pebble investigation needs an explicit selection method and consistent measurements. Define the stretch of beach and the comparison being tested. Systematic sampling can select positions at stated intervals from a stated start; random sampling uses a chance procedure linked to eligible positions; stratified sampling selects within relevant groups under a declared allocation. These methods address different coverage issues. Choosing the nearest attractive pebble is not random. A quadrat placed at each sample point marks the area from which pebbles are chosen. Size is measured with a ruler or callipers, and shape with a pebbleometer or a roundness chart.

before.heading: Longshore drift
before.text: Longshore drift is the net transport of beach material along the coast through oblique swash and returning backwash. Waves are driven by the wind, so they usually approach the shore at the angle of the prevailing wind, and the swash runs diagonally up the beach. Gravity then returns backwash more directly downslope. Repeated movements give sediment a zigzag path with a net alongshore component. The direction depends on wave approach and the orientation of the shore; it is not invariably north, south or to the right of a page. Namibia's five perennial rivers, the Kunene, Okavango, Kwando, Zambezi and Orange, lie along or cross its borders and are fed by rain in neighbouring countries. Interior rivers are ephemeral: they flow for only hours or days after heavy rain, then sink into their sandy beds. A dry channel can carry a large flow after rain in its catchment; a single dry observation does not establish that it never floods.

before.text: Major Namibian dams include Hardap, Naute, Neckartal, Von Bach, Swakoppoort and Omatako. Dams give a store for dry periods, irrigation, flood control and recreation, but flood land, may displace people, lose much water to evaporation, reduce flow downstream and can spread bilharzia, which freshwater snails in still water transmit.

before.heading: The Stevenson screen
before.text: A Stevenson screen is an instrument shelter designed to help measure representative air temperature and humidity while reducing direct effects of sunshine, precipitation and nearby heated surfaces. The familiar school model is a raised, white, louvred enclosure. Its slatted sides allow air circulation while shielding instruments. The white exterior reflects much incoming solar radiation, reducing heating of the shelter relative to a darker surface under similar conditions. A roof provides protection from direct radiation and precipitation; designs can include a double roof to reduce heat transfer. The screen is traditionally made of wood, a poor conductor of heat, so the box itself passes little of the sun’s heat to the instruments; modern shelters may use other insulating materials.

before.prompt: How far do you agree that churches play an important part in reducing the impact of HIV and AIDS in Namibia?
before.canonical_answer: Agree to a large extent. About 90% of Namibians are Christian, so churches reach many people. They provide counselling, home visits and care for the sick, help orphans with food and school costs, and can reduce stigma and encourage testing; some faith-based institutions also provide treatment. However, churches cannot replace medical services, and some religious messages discourage condom use or present HIV as a moral failing, which can increase stigma. Their role is important mainly in care and support, alongside health services.

before.text: Internal migration redistributes population and service needs. An urban destination can gain working-age residents and demand for housing, transport or schools. An origin can lose labour while receiving remittances or later return migrants with skills. The balance depends on who moves, duration, employment and ties. Windhoek shows this. Khomas region grew from 342,141 people in 2011 to 494,605 in 2023, an increase of 44.6%, putting pressure on housing, water, sanitation and jobs.

before.prompt: “Poor transport is the main problem limiting the development of tourism in Namibia.” How far do you agree with this statement?
before.canonical_answer: Partly agree. For the statement: attractions such as Etosha, Sossusvlei and Fish River Canyon are far apart and far from overseas markets; most roads are gravel or earth, so journeys are slow and costly; and the closure of Air Namibia in 2021 ended its own Frankfurt service, although other airlines continue direct international services. Against it: transport is only one constraint. Lodges also need capital for buildings, water and waste systems; marketing is needed to attract bookings; trained staff and good organisation are needed to deliver services; and seasonal demand leaves facilities underused. Decision: poor transport is a major problem, especially for remote sites, but it works together with capital, marketing and management problems, so it is not on its own the main problem.
marking_guidance: Up to 4 C marks for a judgement using Namibian transport evidence (distance, gravel roads, air links) weighed against other constraints (capital, marketing, organisation, seasonality).
1 C mark for a supported overall decision.

before.text: Transport constraints include distance, road condition, limited services, journey time and the cost of reaching an attraction. An unsuitable access route can discourage visits or make supplies expensive. Improvements may include maintaining routes, coordinating transfers, providing clear information or suitable shared transport. The choice should consider environmental sensitivity and resident needs. A new road can improve access while increasing pressure on a previously quiet site, so development requires linked capacity and management decisions. In Namibia, attractions such as Etosha, Sossusvlei and Fish River Canyon are far apart and far from overseas markets. Most roads are gravel or earth rather than tar, so journeys to remote lodges are slow and hard on vehicles. Air access is limited: the national airline stopped flying in February 2021, which reduced air links and left long-haul routes to foreign airlines. Possible solutions include tarring key routes, attracting other airlines and offering clear road information for self-drive visitors.

before.text: Velocity is speed of flow, commonly expressed in metres per second. Discharge is volume passing a cross-section per unit time, commonly cubic metres per second. The two are related through cross-sectional area but are not identical. A channel can become wider and deeper as discharge increases, so a change in volume does not determine velocity without considering channel geometry. Likewise, a narrow constriction may have rapid flow even where the river’s overall gradient is gentle. Volume still matters for deposition. When the volume of water falls, the river has less energy and can no longer carry all its load, so it deposits some of it. Volume falls in the dry season and after a flood, when water evaporates in hot, dry areas, when it seeps into a sandy or permeable bed, and when people abstract it. Many Namibian rivers are ephemeral and lose water as they flow. During the floods studied on the Kuiseb River in the Namib, the water shrank downstream and all the transported material was deposited in the lower river; no water or sediment reached the Atlantic Ocean.

Likewise, a narrow constriction may have rapid flow even where the river’s overall gradient is gentle. Volume still matters for deposition. When flow weakens enough to reduce sediment-transport capacity, a river deposits some of its load; water loss can contribute to this, depending on channel conditions. A supplied safe survey compares beaches A and B. H1: A has a steeper overall surveyed profile than B. H2: A is wider than B at the comparable reference level. A profile data (distance m, height m): (0,0), (10,0.5), (20,1.5), (30,3). B: (0,0), (10,0.3), (20,1). Heights were worked out from the field angle and distance readings. Width repeats: A 30,32,31 m; B 20,22,21 m. The profile plot must use the supplied axes: distance 0–30 m, height 0–3 m. Use provided data; do not enter hazardous water.
(a) Name the instrument used to measure a beach-slope angle. [1]
(b) Describe the sequence producing longshore drift. [3]
(c) Name two pieces of equipment, other than a clinometer, used to survey a beach profile. [2]
(d) Calculate A’s overall gradient as a ratio with both distances in metres. [3]
(e) Describe the A/B profile pattern using values. [3]
(f) What conclusion about H1 is supported, with a limitation? [3]
(g) What conclusion about H2 is supported, with a limitation? [3]
(h) Design a repeatable profile procedure using the same reference conditions. [3]
(i) Describe how distance and angle readings would be recorded consistently. [3]
(j) Complete the field-record headings for the two variables needed for each profile segment, including units. [2]
(k) Plot A’s four supplied points on the provided axes. [2]
(l) Explain why comparable tide/reference conditions matter. [2]

(a) Clinometer. (b) Waves driven by the prevailing wind approach at an angle, so swash moves material diagonally up the beach; backwash returns it straight downslope; repeated cycles produce net alongshore displacement. (c) Ranging poles and a tape measure. (d) Vertical/horizontal = 3/30 = 0.1, equivalent to gradient 1:10. (e) A rises 3 m over 30 m; B 1 m over 20 m, making A steeper overall in these surveys. (f) H1 is supported by 1:10 versus 1:20; these are sampled profiles, not every place/date. (g) All supplied A widths exceed B, supporting H2 for the comparable measurements; the sample does not establish all-season widths. (h) Fixed start, defined shore-normal line and consistent pole/segment method under approved safe comparable conditions. (i) Record positions, distances and signed angles with consistent pole reference heights and units, retaining repeats or errors transparently. (j) Segment distance (m); slope angle (degrees). (k) Correct coordinates are (0,0),(10,0.5),(20,1.5),(30,3), connected in order. (l) Water level changes apparent width/reference positions, so comparable conditions reduce a timing/measurement confound.

marking_guidance: (a) 1 A for clinometer; (b) 3 A for wind-driven oblique swash, backwash straight downslope and repeated net movement; (c) 2 A, one each for ranging poles and tape measure (accept compass for transect direction).
(d) 3 B: method vertical/horizontal in equal units, 3/30 simplification, correct 1:10 ratio. (e) 3 B: A values, B values and the comparative interpretation.

(f) 3 C: supported hypothesis H1 conclusion, comparative gradient evidence and evaluation of sampled-profile limitations. (g) 3 C: supported hypothesis H2 conclusion, repeated width evidence and limited-period coverage.
(h) 3 D: reference/line, consistent equipment/segment procedure, approved safe/comparable conditions. (i) 3 D: traceable position record, consistent distance/angle procedure, signs/units/repeats.

(j) 2 D: one per correct variable heading with unit. (k) 2 D: accurate supplied-coordinate plotting and appropriate ordered connection on the supplied axes; no credit merely for rewriting the list. (l) 2 D: reason linking tide to width/reference and the resulting comparability.

A safe supplied pebble survey uses the same selection rule and three observations per site. H1: mean longest-axis size increases northward. H2: the proportion classed rounded increases northward. Sites at northward distances 0,10,20 m have sizes (18,20,22), (28,30,32), (38,40,42) mm. Rounded counts out of three are 0,1,0. Use a supplied roundness scale consistently. The plot axes are northward distance 0–20 m and mean size 0–50 mm.
(a) Name the erosion process involving load-particle collisions and rounding. [1]
(b) Describe its contact and change sequence. [3]
(c) Name two different pebble variables that must be kept separate. [2]
(d) Calculate mean size at the 0 m site. [3]
(e) Describe the size and rounded-count patterns. [3]
(f) What conclusion on H1 is supported, with a limitation? [3]
(g) What conclusion on H2 is supported, with a limitation? [3]
(h) Design systematic selection along the measured stretch, including a starting rule and no-suitable-pebble rule. [3]
(i) Describe how size and shape would be measured and recorded consistently. [3]
(j) Complete the headings for the measurement unit of size and the stated shape classification. [2]
(k) Plot mean size at all three sites on the supplied axes. [2]
(l) Explain why a larger sample alone does not fix biased selection. [2]
before.canonical_answer:
(a) Attrition. (b) Transported particles collide, corners/fragments are removed and particles can become smaller/rounder. (c) Size and roundness/shape. (d) (18+20+22)/3 = 20 mm. (e) Mean size rises 20→30→40 mm, while rounded counts rise then fall 0→1→0. (f) H1 is supported at these sites; source differences and the small/date-specific sample limit a broader claim. (g) H2’s steady increase is not supported; the middle peak and equal end counts contradict it, though three pebbles per site give weak wider coverage. (h) State a start and regular interval, apply an unbiased fixed local selection rule and predeclare treatment when no eligible pebble is present. (i) Measure the same (longest) axis with a ruler or callipers in mm, use the same roundness scale and record each result against position. (j) Longest-axis size (mm); rounded/not rounded according to the supplied scale. (k) (0,20),(10,30),(20,40). (l) Repeating a biased choice can increase the count while retaining systematic exclusion or preference.

![Mean sizes 20, 30 and 40 mm plotted and record headings completed](../../../assets/images/ITEM-6137-1.5-P05-VIS-6137-1.5-06-answer.png)
marking_guidance: (a) 1 A for attrition; (b) 3 A for collision, corner loss and size/rounding result; (c) 2 A for size and shape.
(d) 3 B: correct total/three-observation method, 20 result and mm unit. (e) 3 B for the size trend with values, non-monotonic rounded counts and explicit contrast between variables.
(f) 3 C: supported decision, size evidence and evaluation of sample/source limitations. (g) 3 C: hypothesis H2 rejection conclusion, middle/end evidence and small-sample limitation.
(h) 3 D: start/interval, consistent eligible selection, predeclared absence rule. (i) 3 D: axis/units, shared shape scale, position-linked record.

(j) 2 D for correct size unit and shape heading/classification. (k) 2 D for accurate three-point plotting and clear trend representation on supplied axes. (l) 2 D for the reason that bias is systematic and its persistence despite more observations.

![Blank axes for signed displacement (−2 to +5 m, north positive) against trial 1 to 5, with blank totals for recovered and unrecovered trials](../../../assets/images/ITEM-6137-1.5-P06-VIS-6137-1.5-07-question.png)

Supplied movement observations use an approved safe method, a fixed origin and equal two-minute intervals. Positive displacement is north. H1: mean recovered displacement is northward. H2: recovered displacement increases in every successive trial. Trials 1–5 record +2,+4,+1,−1 m, and not recovered. The plot axes are trial 1–5 and signed displacement −2 to +5 m; non-recovery is not a plotted zero.
(a) Name the net alongshore sediment-transport process. [1]
(b) Describe its swash/backwash sequence. [3]
(c) Name two variables needed to report displacement clearly. [2]
(d) Calculate the mean signed displacement of recovered observations. [3]
(e) Describe the recovered pattern and exception. [3]
(f) What conclusion on H1 is supported, with a limitation? [3]
(g) What conclusion on H2 is supported, with a limitation? [3]
(h) Design repeated movement observations with a defined reference and safe approved method. [3]
(i) Describe a record that distinguishes recovery, zero and unknown positions. [3]
(j) Complete the totals for recovered and unrecovered trials. [2]
(k) Plot recovered signed displacements on supplied axes, leaving non-recovery distinct. [2]
(l) Explain why replacing non-recovery with zero could mislead. [2]
before.canonical_answer:
(a) Longshore drift. (b) Waves driven by the prevailing wind approach at an angle, so swash carries sediment diagonally up the beach; return backwash moves downslope; repetition produces net alongshore movement. (c) Distance and direction. (d) (2+4+1−1)/4 = +1.5 m, northward. (e) Three northward records and one southward record; values do not increase steadily. (f) H1 is supported by the positive mean among recovered observations; missing trial 5 and short coverage limit the inference. (g) H2 is not supported: +4 falls to +1 and then −1; unknown trial 5 cannot repair the documented decreases. (h) State origin/direction and equal duration, repeat the approved observation method and retain safety/environmental constraints. (i) Record trial/time, position or signed distance/direction and recovery status; zero is a known unchanged position while unknown is missing. (j) Four recovered, one unrecovered. (k) Plot (1,2),(2,4),(3,1),(4,−1); mark trial 5 as missing separately. (l) Unknown position could have moved either way; inventing zero changes the mean and may distort the decision.

![Recovered displacements plotted, trial 5 marked not recovered, and totals completed](../../../assets/images/ITEM-6137-1.5-P06-VIS-6137-1.5-07-answer.png)
marking_guidance: (a) 1 A for longshore drift; (b) 3 A for wind-driven oblique swash, backwash straight downslope and repeated net alongshore movement; (c) 2 A for distance and direction.
(d) 3 B: signed-sum method 6/4, +1.5 result, m/north direction. (e) 3 B for the positive majority, negative exception and non-increasing sequence using the data.

(f) 3 C: hypothesis H1 conclusion for recovered data, positive-mean evidence, evaluation of missing/short-period limitations. (g) 3 C: hypothesis H2 rejection conclusion, documented decreases and correct treatment of unknown trial.
(h) 3 D: fixed reference, equal repeated interval/method, safe approved constraints. (i) 3 D: trial-linked measurements, direction-aware values, separate recovery/zero/unknown record.

(j) 2 D for four recovered and one missing. (k) 2 D for correct signed plotting and distinct missing-data treatment on supplied axes. (l) 2 D for the unknown-versus-zero reason and its effect on estimates/conclusions.

![Blank paired before-and-after axes for mean width (0 to 35 m) at reaches U, D and C](../../../assets/images/ITEM-6137-1.5-P07-VIS-6137-1.5-08-question.png)

A hypothetical groyne investigation compares a southern updrift reach U, northern downdrift reach D and a reference reach C. Repeated surveys use comparable tide/reference conditions. H1: U gains more width than C. H2: D does not narrow. Mean widths before→after are D 18→10 m and C 20→19 m. U’s mean width before was 20 m; its three after readings are 29, 30 and 31 m. Wave/tracer observations support northward transport. Use supplied before/after plotting axes: reach U,D,C and width 0–35 m.
(a) Name the uprush after wave breaking. [1]
(b) Describe how a groyne can affect longshore sediment supply. [3]
(c) Name two pieces of equipment needed to measure beach width along a fixed transect. [2]
(d) Using U’s mean after width from part (j), calculate its percentage width increase, with the before width as denominator. [3]
(e) Describe the before/after contrasts across the three reaches. [3]
(f) What conclusion on H1 is supported, with a limitation? [3]
(g) What conclusion on H2 is supported, with a limitation? [3]
(h) Design a repeatable survey to test future width changes, including a suitable comparison. [3]
(i) Describe how to control or record tide/reference and transect differences. [3]
(j) Complete U’s mean after width and its unit from the three readings. [2]
(k) Plot the before/after widths for U,D,C on the supplied axes. [2]
(l) Explain why the reference reach helps but does not prove a unique cause. [2]
before.canonical_answer:
(a) Swash. (b) A groyne intercepts some alongshore material, encouraging updrift accumulation and potentially reducing onward supply. before.heading: Longshore drift
before.text: Longshore drift is the net transport of beach material along the coast through oblique swash and returning backwash. Waves are driven by the wind, so they usually approach the shore at the angle of the prevailing wind, and the swash runs diagonally up the beach. Gravity then returns backwash more directly downslope. Repeated movements give sediment a zigzag path with a net alongshore component. The direction depends on wave approach and the orientation of the shore; it is not invariably north, south or to the right of a page. Net drift is therefore usually in the general direction of the prevailing wind along that coast. A labelled diagram shows the prevailing wind, the oblique swash, the backwash running straight down the beach and an arrow for the direction of drift. Longshore currents can also transport sediment within the nearshore system.
before.reviewed_unchanged: Codex independently checked this artefact against revised claim text; content remains consistent unless separately logged as repaired.

after.heading: Longshore drift
after.text: Longshore drift is the net transport of beach material along the coast through oblique swash and returning backwash. When breaking waves approach the shore obliquely, swash runs diagonally up the beach. Gravity then returns backwash more directly downslope. Repeated movements give sediment a zigzag path with a net alongshore component. The direction depends on wave approach and the orientation of the shore; it is not invariably north, south or to the right of a page. Local wind can influence wave direction, but distant swell and refraction mean drift cannot always be inferred from the local wind. A labelled diagram shows the prevailing wind, the oblique swash, the backwash running straight down the beach and an arrow for the direction of drift. Longshore currents can also transport sediment within the nearshore system.

A coastal teaching trial releases five tracers and observes safely from shore for a defined one-minute interval. North is positive. Four are recovered at +3,+2,−1,+4 m; the fifth is missing. H1: every released tracer moves north. H2: mean displacement of recovered tracers is northward. The supplied signed plan and recording sheet retain the missing value. Provided axes have tracer categories A/B/C/D and displacement −2 to +5 m.
(a) Name alongshore sediment transport associated with oblique swash and return flow. [1]
(b) Describe three relevant links in that transport mechanism. [3]
(c) Name two beach conditions needing consideration in safe matched observations. [2]
(d) Calculate mean displacement of the recovered tracers with direction. [3]
(e) Describe three distinct movement/coverage features. [3]
(f) What conclusion about H1 is supported? [3]
(g) What conclusion about H2 is supported? [3]
(h) Design a safe test of the two hypotheses. [3]
(i) Describe a signed measurement and recording sequence. [3]
(j) Complete the recovered count and signed total on the supplied sheet. [2]
(k) Plot tracers C and D on the provided axes. [2]
(l) Explain the missing-tracer limitation and a suitable improvement. [2]
before.canonical_answer:
(a) Longshore drift. (b) Oblique swash moves sediment up the beach; return flow carries it downslope; repeated movements can create net alongshore transfer. (c) Tide, waves, weather or shore access: two relevant safe-condition examples. (d) (3+2−1+4)/4 = +2 m, northward. (e) Three recovered values are north, one south, and one of five releases has unknown displacement; recovered net is +8 m. Credit three distinct features. (f) H1 is rejected because one recovered tracer goes south and the missing one cannot be assigned north. (g) H2 is supported for the recovered subset by the +2 m mean, not for every release or later interval. (h) Retain both measurable predictions, a safe eligible shore observation design, matched duration and a feasible recovery/recording plan without entering dangerous water. (i) Fix reference and sign, measure signed positions consistently, record each recovery and missing status before the mean. (j) Four recovered; +8 m total. (k) C −1 m; D +4 m. (l) Missing displacement limits all-release inference; suitable repeated safe trials and better feasible recovery coverage can strengthen later evidence, without entering zero for missing.

A tourism teaching investigation compares managed M and reference R over matched before/after periods. Pollution score: zero least, five most. M changes 4→2; R changes 3→4. Visitor counts at each site rise 10→40. A new collection arrangement starts at M, but weather and other actions are not fully controlled. H1: recorded pollution falls at M. H2: recorded pollution falls at R. Supplied sheets retain scale direction and periods; provided plotting axes have before/after categories and pollution scores 0–5 with site key.
(a) Name one tourism waste pressure. [1]
(b) Describe three functions of suitable visitor-site management. [3]
(c) Name two possible influences on observed pollution besides the new arrangement. [2]
(d) Calculate the numerical score reduction at M, with scale units. [3]
(e) Describe three distinct paired patterns using data. [3]
(f) What conclusion about H1 and causal attribution is supported? [3]
(g) What conclusion about H2 is supported? [3]
(h) Design a test using the two hypotheses and reference comparison. [3]
(i) Describe a consistent score/count record sequence. [3]
(j) Complete R’s score change and the direction of its condition on the supplied sheet. [2]
(k) Plot M’s before/after scores on the provided axes. [2]
(l) Explain one specific limitation and a matched improvement. [2]
before.canonical_answer:
(a) Litter or a relevant pollution pressure. (b) Any three, e.g.: bins are provided and emptied often enough to stop litter building up; paths are marked and maintained so visitors do not trample vegetation; visitor numbers or access times are controlled at busy places; toilets and water supply are kept working so waste does not reach the environment. (c) Weather, cleaning timing, other users or changing recording: two relevant factors. (d) 4−2 = 2 score points on the stated pollution scale. (e) M improves from four to two, R worsens from three to four, and visitor counts rise at both sites. (f) H1 is supported by the lower pollution score, but other unmeasured influences prevent assigning the entire improvement to the new arrangement. (g) H2 is rejected: R’s score rises by one, indicating worse recorded pollution under this key. (h) State both predictions, retain comparable reference/managed sites and matched periods, and record relevant context. (i) Apply common anchors and observation boundaries, count visitors over equal durations and retain separate raw site/period records. (j) +1 score point; worse condition. (k) M before four and after two. (l) Unmatched cleaning/weather could affect scores; match or record them and repeat comparable periods.

before.canonical_answer: Most interior channels are ephemeral and flow briefly after rain. High evaporation removes much water from open reservoirs. Boreholes and wells can tap water stored underground, protected from direct open-water evaporation. Where aquifer storage, recharge, quality and abstraction permit, this sustains farms and settlements through dry periods; boreholes can still fail or be depleted.

before.text: Coastal desalination can add supply where a saline source and suitable infrastructure are available. Since 2010 a reverse-osmosis plant near Wlotzkasbaken, north of Swakopmund, has supplied water that the national water utility delivers to Swakopmund, nearby uranium mines and other parts of the Erongo Region. Delivering that water inland or to higher ground adds pumping and network needs. Energy cost and reliability affect operation. A coast's length alone does not establish a feasible national supply to every settlement. Assess intended volume, location, delivery and environmental effects rather than assuming the ocean removes all scarcity.

after.text: Coastal desalination can add supply where a saline source and suitable infrastructure are available. A reverse-osmosis plant near Wlotzkasbaken, north of Swakopmund, opened in 2010. NamWater contracted to receive its desalinated water in 2013; its 2024 report describes the plant supplying the coastal network and uranium mines. Delivering that water inland or to higher ground adds pumping and network needs. Energy cost and reliability affect operation. A coast's length alone does not establish a feasible national supply to every settlement. Assess intended volume, location, delivery and environmental effects rather than assuming the ocean removes all scarcity.

before.text: Away from the border rivers, most farms and many towns depend on boreholes, because groundwater is available all year and is not lost to evaporation as dam water is. Along the border, the Kunene alone supplies water to about 35 per cent of Namibia's population. Surface storage may collect episodic inflow for later urban or agricultural use. Both require appropriate extraction, treatment and delivery. A pump failure or damaged pipeline can interrupt access even when the source retains water, so physical scarcity and infrastructure failure should be explained separately.

after.text: Away from the border rivers, most farms and many towns depend on boreholes, because usable aquifers can retain water through dry periods and are protected from direct open-water evaporation, subject to storage, recharge, quality and abstraction. Along the border, the Kunene alone supplies water to about 35 per cent of Namibia's population. Surface storage may collect episodic inflow for later urban or agricultural use. Both require appropriate extraction, treatment and delivery. A pump failure or damaged pipeline can interrupt access even when the source retains water, so physical scarcity and infrastructure failure should be explained separately.

before.text: Ruacana on the Kunene River is Namibia's named hydroelectric example. It is a run-of-river station: it has little storage, so its output follows the river's flow. The Kunene rises in Angola, where the rain falls, and it supplies up to 45 per cent of Namibia's electricity. When the river is low in the dry season, Ruacana generates less and Namibia must use other stations or imports.

after.text: Ruacana on the Kunene River is Namibia's named hydroelectric example. It is a run-of-river station: it has little storage, so its output follows the river's flow. before.text: Namibia's five perennial rivers (Kunene, Okavango, Kwando/Linyanti/Chobe, Zambezi and Orange) all lie on or cross its borders and are fed by rain in neighbouring countries; interior rivers are ephemeral and flow only briefly after heavy rain. Major aquifers include the Karst area, Stampriet and Ohangwena, reached by tens of thousands of boreholes and wells. Evaporation (about 2,000 mm a year at the coast to over 3,400 mm in the south-east) far exceeds rainfall.

before.text: Precipitation can infiltrate the soil and, under suitable conditions, move deeper to recharge groundwater. The rate and amount depend on rainfall, soil, geology, vegetation and previous moisture conditions. Not all rain becomes recharge: some evaporates, is used by plants, runs off or remains temporarily in the soil. In Namibia potential evaporation, from about 2,000 mm a year at the coast to over 3,400 mm in the south-east, is far higher than rainfall, so only a small part of the rain recharges aquifers.
